report:
## Research Findings

The claim is actually **well-supported by evidence**, not false. The key study addressing this is a systematic review and meta-analysis by Kappelmann, Lewis, Dantzer, Jones, and Khandaker (published in *Molecular Psychiatry*), which pooled clinical trial data involving over 5,000 participants with chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis) where anti-cytokine drugs (including anti-TNF agents) were tested, with depressive symptoms measured as a secondary outcome ([PMC5794896](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/)).

The meta-analysis found that anti-cytokine treatment produced antidepressant effects of small-to-moderate size—comparable to effect sizes seen with conventional antidepressants ([Pharmaceutical Journal](https://pharmaceutical-journal.com/article/news/anti-inflammatory-drugs-could-treat-symptoms-of-depression)). Notably, the improvement in depressive symptoms did not appear to simply track improvement in the underlying physical illness; the authors reported a lack of correlation between changes in depressive symptoms and changes in primary physical illness severity, which they argue points toward a more direct role for inflammatory cytokines in depression rather than the mood benefit being an artifact of "feeling physically better" ([PMC5794896](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/)).

This finding has been corroborated in follow-up literature; a 2021 paper in *Molecular Psychiatry* on inflammation, depression, and anxiety cites this same meta-analysis as supporting evidence for inflammatory involvement in depression ([Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41380-021-01188-w)).

## Conclusion

Based on the available evidence, the claim is **supported, not false**. Multiple independent secondary sources (New Scientist, CNN, Live Science) and the primary peer-reviewed meta-analysis converge on the same conclusion: anti-cytokine drugs show consistent, modest antidepressant effects in people with chronic inflammatory conditions, beyond what would be expected from disease improvement alone.
